meta.title: Who really said "She Speaks Eighteen Languages, and Can't Say No in Any of Them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Alexander Woollcott printed it; Dorothy Parker said it. The line is on page 149 of While Rome Burns (1934) — and a close variant ran in 1931.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'She Speaks Eighteen Languages, and Can't Say No in Any of Them'?
meta.ogDescription: Woollcott wrote it down, but credited Parker. Verified on page 149 of While Rome Burns (1934), with an earlier 1931 newspaper variant.

answer.label: Not Alexander Woollcott — actually Dorothy Parker
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and Algonquin Round Table wit
answer.sourceLine: The sentence really does sit in Alexander Woollcott’s prose — but inside quotation marks. In his profile Our Mrs. Parker, first printed in Hearst’s International-Cosmopolitan in August 1933 and reprinted in While Rome Burns ↗ (Viking Press, first published March 1934) at page 149, Woollcott reports Parker murmuring it about a guest she has just seen off with enormous warmth. Woollcott is the recorder, not the wit — and even Parker’s claim rests on his single report, since Quote Investigator ↗ found a close variant already in print in 1931 under another byline.

source.excerpt: That woman speaks eighteen languages, and can’t say No in any of them.
trail: 8 September 1931 — a close variant runs in the Chicago Daily Tribune column “A Line O’ Type Or Two” by Richard Henry Little, about a former child prodigy who never learned to say “No” in any of her twelve languages. Not credited to Parker. Quote Investigator ↗

August 1933 — Alexander Woollcott’s profile “Our Mrs. Parker” appears in Hearst’s International-Cosmopolitan. This is the first known ascription of the gibe to Dorothy Parker; Quote Investigator verified the citation from photocopies. Quote Investigator ↗

March 1934 — the same words are reprinted in Woollcott’s essay collection While Rome Burns (The Viking Press), on page 149. We confirmed the sentence in a full-text scan of the Viking text. Internet Archive ↗
2003 — Gene Shalit’s Great Hollywood Wit prints a version naming Merle Oberon as the target, a detail absent from Woollcott. Quote Investigator ↗
source.excerptNote: In Woollcott’s telling, Parker delivers this out of the corner of her mouth, moments after waving a departing guest off with effusive warmth — the whole point of the anecdote being the gap between the two performances. The sentence is Parker’s; the surrounding prose is Woollcott’s.

source.rightsNote: The remark itself was spoken, but the text that fixes it is Woollcott’s: first published in Hearst’s International-Cosmopolitan in August 1933 and in While Rome Burns in March 1934, both after 1930, so we treat the passage as in copyright in the United States. The book’s copyright page reads “Copyright 1934 by Alexander Woollcott”; we have not checked whether that copyright was renewed, so a public-domain claim would be unsafe. The thirteen-word quotation is reproduced here as a short critical quotation with full attribution.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: Dorothy Parker
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
author.bio: Dorothy Parker was an American poet, literary critic and writer of fiction, later a screenwriter, and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table — the New York lunch circle that also included Robert Benchley, Franklin P. Adams and Alexander Woollcott. She wrote theatre criticism for Vanity Fair and drama reviews and light verse for The New Yorker, and her reputation as a wisecracker — one she reportedly deplored — rests heavily on remarks that were spoken rather than published. That is precisely the problem with this quotation: the wit is hers by report, and the paper is Woollcott’s.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: This line is usually printed as Dorothy Parker’s, and that is right. Where it drifts to Alexander Woollcott, the cause is mechanical rather than mischievous: the sentence lives in his book, so indexes organised by book hand it to him.

items.why: The sentence appears in Woollcott’s prose, but in quotation marks, as something Parker says about a departing guest. Wikiquote ↗ files it on Parker’s page under the heading for quotes taken from Woollcott’s essay, and his own Wikiquote page ↗ does not list it among his lines. Quote aggregators indexing by title still surface it on the While Rome Burns quotations page ↗, where it is credited to Parker but sits inside Woollcott’s book.

Quote Investigator ↗ found a close variant in Little’s Chicago Daily Tribune column of 8 September 1931 — before any known ascription to Parker — about a prodigy who never learned to say “No” in any of her twelve languages and married whenever it was suggested. QI does not settle whether Little reworked a Parker quip or Parker’s version was a bawdier reworking of Little’s.
Gene Shalit’s 2003 Great Hollywood Wit prints a version naming the actress, per Quote Investigator ↗. Woollcott names no one; QI calls the polyglot Winifred Sackville Stoner Jr. the solid candidate.

misattribution.truthLine: Parker said it, by Woollcott’s account, and his 1933 profile is the earliest known source for her version — but a close variant was already in print in 1931 ↗ under Richard Henry Little’s byline.

context.heading: Why this one is worth untangling
lead: Woollcott’s profile is one of the great load-bearing documents of American quotation. English Wikiquote notes that “Our Mrs Parker” ↗ is the original published source for some of the best-known comments Parker made at the Algonquin Round Table — which means a handful of the most-repeated lines in the language reach us through one admiring friend’s memory of what was muttered across a lunch table.

That is why the credit slides. The words are printed over Woollcott’s byline, in Woollcott’s book, so quote lists that index by book rather than by speaker quietly hand him the joke. Read the actual page and the ownership is unambiguous: Parker says it, and Woollcott is the one repeating it with obvious relish.
context.detailsSummary: The 1931 version, the Merle Oberon version, and the Gershwin echo
detailsBody: 1931, Chicago. Quote Investigator found the joke’s earliest documented form in the Chicago Daily Tribune column “A Line O’ Type Or Two” of 8 September 1931, written by Richard Henry Little. His target was the former child prodigy Winifred Sackville Stoner Jr. ↗, whose linguistic feats were much publicised and whose marriages were many; Little’s gag is about the altar, not the bedroom.

2003, Hollywood. Gene Shalit’s Great Hollywood Wit prints a version naming the actress Merle Oberon as the woman Parker was skewering. Quote Investigator records this as a late arrival and does not endorse it; no earlier source ties Oberon to the remark.

1942, Broadway. Wikiquote notes a family resemblance in Ira Gershwin’s lyric for “The Saga of Jenny” in Lady in the Dark: a line about a woman who could not say no in twenty-seven languages. A cousin of the joke, not a source for it.
context.pull: The wit is Parker’s. The paper trail is Woollcott’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator documents a 1931 Chicago Daily Tribune variant by Richard Henry Little about Winifred Stoner Jr., names Woollcott's August 1933 Hearst's International-Cosmopolitan profile 'Our Mrs. Parker' (page 90) as the first known ascription to Dorothy Parker, notes the 1934 While Rome Burns reprint at page 149 (Viking Press), and records Gene Shalit's 2003 version naming Merle Oberon.

A full-text scan of While Rome Burns (The Viking Press, New York; published March 1934, copyright 1934 by Alexander Woollcott; this printing 1935) contains the sentence 'That woman speaks eighteen languages, and can't say No in any of them.' on the page carrying the running head 'Some Neighbors 149', inside the essay 'SOME NEIGHBORS: IV / OUR MRS. PARKER', which the table of contents lists as beginning on page 142. Woollcott presents the line in quotation marks as Parker's remark about a departing guest.

English Wikiquote lists 'That woman speaks eighteen languages, and can't say No in any of them.' on the Dorothy Parker page under a section for quotes from Alexander Woollcott's essay 'Our Mrs Parker' in While Rome Burns (1934), describes that essay as the original published source for some of Parker's best-known Algonquin Round Table comments, and notes a later similar line by Ira Gershwin in 'The Saga of Jenny' from Lady in the Dark (1942).
English Wikiquote's Alexander Woollcott page does not list the eighteen-languages line among his quotations.

Alexander Woollcott (January 19, 1887 – January 23, 1943) was a critic and commentator for The New Yorker, a drama critic for the New York Times, a member of the Algonquin Round Table, and the author of the 1934 essay collection While Rome Burns.

Dorothy Parker (August 22, 1893 – June 7, 1967) was an American poet, literary critic and writer of fiction, a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, and a contributor to Vanity Fair and The New Yorker.

Winifred Sackville Stoner Jr. (1902–1983) was an American child prodigy known for rhymes and mnemonic verse who spoke several languages from an early age and married several times in adulthood. The page does not mention the Chicago Tribune quip.

Goodreads' quotations page for While Rome Burns lists 'That woman speaks eighteen languages, and can't say No in any of them.' attributed to Dorothy Parker, While Rome Burns — i.e. the line is indexed under Woollcott's book title.
